## Description

This follows up on [Merill's suggestion on #2633](https://github.com/maester365/maester/pull/2633#pullrequestreview-5762591962) to move the nested connection probe into its own internal GitHub helper.

`Connect-MtGitHub` now passes the request URI, authentication headers and shared rate-limit connection to `Invoke-MtGitHubConnectionProbe`. The request and response handling, 30-second connection and operation timeouts, error classification and cooldown transfer remain unchanged. Administration-probe failures still allow the connection to complete. There are no public API or authentication changes.

The existing connection and rate-limit tests cover the explicit inputs, shared connection identity, response/error handling and cooldowns at each probe.

Closes #2674.

## Validation

On Linux / PowerShell 7.6.6 / Pester 5.7.1:

- All 120 focused connection and rate-limit tests passed.
- All 108 connection and rate-limit tests passed against the built module.
- All 31 expanded rate-limit tests also passed against the unchanged base.
- Changed-file PSScriptAnalyzer, module build and output validation passed.

The complete `./powershell/tests/pester.ps1` run reported 7,064 tests, including 93 skips and five failures. All five failures reproduced on unchanged base `bb7a0e8cc`: one console-colour assertion and four Azure request URI assertions. Those failures are outside this change. The GitHub transport tests, including the real loopback timeout fixtures, passed in the full run.

No live GitHub connection was used for validation. Network-dependent tests use mocks or local loopback fixtures.

- [x] My pull request adheres to the code style of this project.
- [ ] My code requires changes to the documentation.
- [x] I have updated the documentation as required.

---
title: Getting started
description: Your first Maester run, how to read the report, and how to go from a one-off check to continuous monitoring.
---

# Getting started

This page takes you from nothing to a first report in about fifteen minutes, then shows the steps most teams take
over the following weeks. Each step links to the full guide.

## Before you start

- **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS.
- **An account that can read your tenant's configuration.** Global Reader is the usual choice. The first time
  you connect, an admin may need to consent to the Microsoft Graph permissions Maester asks for (see
  [Approval required when connecting](connect-maester/readme.md#approval-required-when-connecting)).

By default Maester asks only for read permissions. It does not change anything in your tenant.

## Step 1: Run your first report

```powershell
Install-Module Maester -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

`Connect-Maester` connects to Microsoft Graph. That is enough for the Entra ID tests and most of the others. To
include Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint and the other Microsoft 365 services, connect to all of them:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All
Invoke-Maester
```

Tests for a service you have not connected to are reported as **Skipped**, with the reason, so you can tell which
results are missing and why. See [Installation](installation.mdx) and [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md).

## Step 2: Read the report

When the run finishes, Maester writes an HTML report to the `./test-results` folder and, in an interactive session, opens it. Every test appears with one
of these results:

| Result | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Passed** | The setting matches what the test expects. |
| **Failed** | The setting does not match. The test explains why and how to fix it. |
| **Investigate** | Maester found something a person should look at; it cannot decide on its own. |
| **Skipped** | The test did not run, for example because a service is not connected or a licence is missing. |
| **Error** | The test could not finish, for example because of a missing permission. |

Each failed test links to its own page on this site, with the background, the fix and the references.

## Step 3: Fix what matters first

A first report usually has many failures. Do not try to fix them all at once.

1. **Sort by severity.** Start with **Critical** and **High** (see [Severity levels](configuration/severity-levels.md)).
   To run only those tests:

   ```powershell
   Invoke-Maester -Severity Critical, High
   ```

2. **Look for quick wins.** Each test says how much its fix affects users and how much effort it takes. A failure
   with high severity, low user impact and low cost is the best place to start. In an interactive run, the
   **Fix first** panel lists these failures for you.
3. **Record what you accept.** Some failures are deliberate decisions. Turn those tests off in your configuration
   with a reason, so the report shows them as **Not run** with your reason instead of as failures (see the next
   step).

## Step 4: Tell Maester about your tenant

Create a folder for your Maester settings and a `maester-config.json` in it. The most important setting is your
emergency access (break glass) accounts, which many Conditional Access tests depend on:

```json
{
  "GlobalSettings": {
    "EmergencyAccessAccounts": [
      { "Type": "User", "UserPrincipalName": "BreakGlass1@contoso.com" }
    ]
  },
  "TestSettings": [
    { "Id": "MT.1089", "Enabled": false, "Reason": "Accepted risk, see ticket SEC-123" }
  ]
}
```

Then run Maester from that folder, or pass it with `-Path`:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -Path ./maester
```

See [Configure Maester](configuration/overview.md) and [Emergency access accounts](configuration/emergency-access-accounts.md).

## Step 5: Choose your baseline

Maester ships several suites: its own tests and the CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA suites. Pick the ones that match
the requirements your organisation has to meet. See [Choosing a baseline](choosing-a-baseline.md).

## Step 6: Monitor continuously

A single report shows where you stand today. The value of Maester comes from running it every day, so that a change
that weakens your security is caught within a day instead of at the next audit.

1. Run Maester on a schedule from a pipeline or an Azure service. See [Monitoring with Maester](monitoring/readme.mdx).
2. Send the results to the people who act on them by email, Teams or Slack. See [Maester alerts](alerts/readme.mdx).
3. Export results for a ticketing system or a spreadsheet. See [Exporting results](export-results.md).

## Step 7: Add your own tests

The built-in tests check widely recommended settings. Your organisation also has its own rules: a group that must
always be in a policy, a named location that must exist, an app that must never get more permissions. Write those
rules as [custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx) and Maester checks them on every run alongside the built-in ones.

## Next steps

- Need support from leadership to roll this out? See [Making the case for Maester](making-the-case.mdx).
- Questions? See the [FAQ](faq.md).

title: Choosing a baseline
description: The test suites that ship with Maester, which requirements each one serves, and how to run the combination that fits your organisation.
---

# Choosing a baseline

Maester does not pick a security framework for you. It ships several suites of tests, each built from a different
source, and you run the ones that match the requirements your organisation has to meet. This page explains what
each suite is, helps you match suites to your requirements, and shows how to make your choice the default for every
run.

## The suites that ship with Maester

| Suite | Source | What it checks | `-Suite` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Maester](/docs/tests/maester) | The Maester community | Entra ID, Conditional Access, privileged access, app registrations, Exchange, Teams, Defender, Intune, Azure DevOps, AI agents and more. Written from real attacks and misconfigurations seen in tenants. | `Maester` |
| [CIS](/docs/tests/cis) | [CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark](https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/microsoft_365) and CIS GitHub Benchmark | The benchmark's automatable recommendations. Each test's title starts with its level, **(L1)** or **(L2)**. | `CIS` |
| [CISA](/docs/tests/cisa) | [CISA SCuBA](https://github.com/cisagov/ScubaGear) Secure Configuration Baselines | The automatable SCuBA policies for Entra ID, Exchange Online and SharePoint Online. Each requirement carries its NIST SP 800-53 references. | `CISA` |
| [ASD](/docs/tests/asd) | [ASD Essential Eight maturity model](https://www.cyber.gov.au/business-government/asds-cyber-security-frameworks/essential-eight/essential-eight-maturity-model) and [Information security manual](https://www.cyber.gov.au/ism) (ISM) | Entra ID and Intune settings for the Essential Eight requirements and ISM controls that can be read from Microsoft 365, such as phishing-resistant MFA, just-in-time administration and Office macro hardening. Each result names its ISM control and, for Essential Eight, the maturity level and mitigation strategy. | `ASD` |
| [EIDSCA](/docs/tests/eidsca) | [Entra ID Security Config Analyzer](https://github.com/Cloud-Architekt/AzureAD-Attack-Defense) | Entra ID tenant settings (authorisation, consent, authentication methods, password protection) against recommended values. | `EIDSCA` |
| [ORCA](/docs/tests/orca) | [Office 365 Recommended Configuration Analyzer](https://github.com/cammurray/orca) | Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365: anti-spam, anti-phishing, Safe Links, Safe Attachments. | `ORCA` |
| [Active Directory](/docs/tests/ad) | The Maester community | On-premises Active Directory inventory and configuration. Runs only after `Connect-Maester -Service ActiveDirectory`. | `AD` |

[Maester Packs](packs/index.md) add more, for example the [Zero Trust Assessment pack](packs/zero-trust-assessment.md),
which runs Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment and shows its results in the same report.

By default, `Invoke-Maester` runs every built-in suite except Active Directory, and leaves out preview and
long-running tests.

## Match suites to your requirements

Start from what your organisation has to show, not from the suites. Most organisations combine two or three rows.

| If your requirement is… | Run | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence against the CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark (an auditor, an insurer, a customer questionnaire) | `CIS` | Each result names its CIS recommendation and level. |
| Alignment with CISA SCuBA, or a control set built on NIST SP 800-53 | `CISA` | Each result names its SCuBA policy, and the NIST controls it relates to. |
| Alignment with the ASD Essential Eight or the ISM (Australian government and organisations that follow ASD guidance) | `ASD` | Each result names its ISM control, and for Essential Eight the maturity level (ML1 to ML3) and mitigation strategy. A passing check is evidence for its control, not an Essential Eight assessment. |
| An internal standard, or a framework Maester does not ship (ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, a sector regulation) | `Maester`, `EIDSCA`, plus your own tests mapped to that framework | Maester's tests cover the technical settings most frameworks ask for. Map your own tests to your framework's requirements (see [below](#your-own-framework)). |
| Hardening Entra ID against identity attacks | `Maester`, `EIDSCA` | Conditional Access, privileged access, consent and authentication settings. |
| Reducing phishing and malware by email | `ORCA`, and the Exchange and Defender tests of `Maester` | Mail flow protection and its policies. |
| A Zero Trust programme | The [Zero Trust Assessment pack](packs/zero-trust-assessment.md) and `Maester` | Microsoft's assessment by Zero Trust pillar, with Maester's checks in the same report. |
| Hybrid identity with on-premises Active Directory | `AD`, alongside the others | The on-premises side of the identity that Entra ID trusts. |
| No formal requirement yet | Everything (the default) | You see the whole picture and narrow it down later. |

### Overlap between suites

Several suites check the same setting from their own source. For example, blocking legacy authentication is
checked by [MT.1009](/docs/tests/MT.1009), [CIS.M365.5.2.2.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.2.2.3) and the CISA
suite. That is expected: each result reports against its own framework. If you need only one view, run the suite
that matches your requirement and fill gaps from the others with `-TestId`.

## Make your choice the default

Run a combination on the command line:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -Suite CIS, Maester
```

Or save it in the `Selection` section of `maester-config.json`, so every run, including scheduled ones, uses the
same baseline:

```json
{
  "Selection": {
    "Suite": ["CIS", "Maester"]
  }
}
```

Selectors combine: values of one selector are alternatives, different selectors must all match. To focus on the most
urgent tests of your baseline first:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -Suite CISA -Severity Critical, High
```

See the [run configuration reference](configuration/run-configuration.md) for every key of `Selection`, and
[Invoke-Maester](commands/Invoke-Maester.mdx) for all the selectors (`-Product`, `-Feature`, `-Area`, `-Severity`,
`-Suite`, `-TestId`).

## Adapt the baseline to your organisation

No baseline fits an organisation without changes. Record your decisions in `maester-config.json`, so they are
visible and reviewed rather than ignored:

- **A recommendation you have decided not to follow:** turn the test off with a reason. The report shows it as
  **Not run** with your reason, so an auditor can see the decision.
- **A risk that matters more or less to you:** change the test's severity.
- **A threshold that differs from the default:** change the test's parameters.

```json
{
  "TestSettings": [
    { "Id": "CIS.M365.1.3.3", "Enabled": false, "Reason": "Calendar sharing approved by risk committee, RISK-042" },
    { "Id": "MT.1005", "Severity": "Critical" },
    { "Id": "MT.1198", "Parameters": { "MaximumValidityDays": 180 } }
  ]
}
```

Keep this file in version control so that every change to your baseline has an author, a date and a review.
See [Configure Maester](configuration/overview.md).

## Your own framework

If your organisation has its own standard, or follows a framework Maester does not ship, write tests for the
requirements Maester does not already cover and map each one to its requirement with the `Control` attribute. A
framework file in your suite gives Maester the framework's name, version and requirements, and every result then
names the requirement it implements. See
[Benchmarks and framework files](writing-tests/index.mdx#benchmarks-and-framework-files).

Many built-in tests already name the NIST SP 800-53 controls they support in their `Control` attribute, and most
frameworks publish a mapping to NIST SP 800-53, which helps you find the built-in tests that serve a requirement.

title: Making the case for Maester
description: Templates to explain to executives, a CISO and an IT Security Adviser why your organisation should monitor its Microsoft 365 configuration with Maester, with examples of what goes unnoticed without it.
---

import { Tabs, TabItem } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

# Making the case for Maester

Maester is free, but rolling it out still needs someone's time, a place to run it and, often, approval. This page
helps you get that approval. It has three parts:

1. [What organisations miss without continuous monitoring](#what-organisations-miss-without-continuous-monitoring):
   real configuration failures, each with the Maester test that catches it. Use them as examples in any of the
   templates.
2. [Templates](#templates) for three audiences: general executives, a CISO, and an IT Security Adviser (ITSA). Copy
   one, replace the text in `[brackets]`, and delete what does not apply.
3. [Common questions](#common-questions) that come up in these conversations, with honest answers.

:::tip[Run Maester first]
The strongest argument is your own tenant. Run Maester once (see [Getting started](getting-started.md)) and quote
your own numbers: how many Critical and High failures there are, and two or three examples from the list below that
you actually found.
:::

## What organisations miss without continuous monitoring

A Microsoft 365 tenant changes every week: people join and leave, admins grant exceptions, projects add apps, and
Microsoft releases new features with new settings. Most security weaknesses in a tenant are not the result of an
attack. They are a setting that was right once, and was then changed, or quietly stopped working, without anyone
noticing. A yearly audit or a one-off assessment sees the tenant on one day. Continuous monitoring sees the day it
changed.

| What goes wrong | Why nobody notices | What it can lead to | Maester checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A Conditional Access policy stops protecting anyone.** The group it targets is deleted, or a user or role it names no longer exists. | The policy still shows as *On* in the portal. Nothing alerts. | Users who should need MFA, or a compliant device, sign in without either. | [MT.1038](/docs/tests/MT.1038), [MT.1066](/docs/tests/MT.1066) |
| **Admins lock themselves out.** An emergency access (break glass) account is caught by a new policy, or blocked. | The account is used only in an emergency, so the problem is found during the emergency. | No way into the tenant during an outage or an incident. | [MT.1005](/docs/tests/MT.1005), [MT.1034](/docs/tests/MT.1034) |
| **Too many people hold the keys.** Global Administrators accumulate; people who left or changed role keep privileged roles. | Role assignments are rarely reviewed, and each one was justified when it was made. | A single phished account can take over the whole tenant. | [MT.1032](/docs/tests/MT.1032), [MT.1029](/docs/tests/MT.1029), [CIS.M365.1.1.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.1.1.3) |
| **MFA is bypassed through legacy authentication.** An exception is added for an old device or app and never removed. | MFA appears to be enforced for everyone. | Password spraying succeeds against accounts that "have MFA". | [MT.1009](/docs/tests/MT.1009), [CISA.MS.AAD.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.AAD.1.1) |
| **Users hand attackers access through an app.** Users can consent to third-party apps that read mail and files. | Consent looks like a normal sign-in prompt to the user. | Persistent access to mailboxes and files that survives a password reset. | [CIS.M365.5.1.5.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.1.5.1), [EIDSCA.AP08](/docs/tests/EIDSCA.AP08) |
| **Mail is forwarded outside the organisation.** Automatic forwarding to external domains is allowed. | Forwarding rules are set per mailbox, often by an attacker after a compromise. | Silent, continuing data loss. | [CISA.MS.EXO.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.1.1) |
| **There is no record when you need it.** Audit logging or mailbox auditing is off. | Logs are only looked at after an incident. | You cannot tell what an attacker did, or meet breach-notification and legal obligations. | [CIS.M365.3.1.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.3.1.1), [CISA.MS.EXO.13.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.13.1) |
| **Anyone can send email as you.** DMARC is missing or not enforced on a domain. | Mail still flows normally. | Invoice fraud and phishing that appears to come from your own domain. | [MT.1182](/docs/tests/MT.1182) |
| **Applications hold powerful, long-lived secrets.** A service principal with a client secret holds a permanent privileged role. | Apps are created by projects and rarely reviewed by security. | A leaked secret gives an attacker admin rights without any user sign-in or MFA. | [MT.1027](/docs/tests/MT.1027), [MT.1057](/docs/tests/MT.1057) |
| **An integration stops working.** An app registration's certificate or secret expires. | The expiry date is in the portal, but nobody is watching it. | An outage of a business process that depends on the app. | [MT.1199](/docs/tests/MT.1199) |
| **Files are shared with anyone.** External sharing is opened up for one project and left open. | Sharing settings are changed in a different admin centre from the rest of security. | Sensitive documents reachable by people outside the organisation. | [CIS.M365.7.2.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.7.2.3) |
| **A new phishing technique works.** Device code sign-in is allowed for everyone. | It is on by default and rarely needed. | Phishing that captures a signed-in session, including MFA. | [CIS.M365.5.2.2.12](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.2.2.12) |

Beyond individual weaknesses, an organisation without continuous monitoring also misses:

- **Early warning.** A weakening change is found within a day, by your team, instead of months later by an auditor,
  a penetration tester or an attacker.
- **Evidence on demand.** Every run is a dated, repeatable record of which controls passed. Audit and assurance
  evidence no longer has to be gathered by hand.
- **Knowledge that stays when people leave.** Your intent ("this group must always be in this policy") is written
  down as a test, not kept in one admin's head.
- **A measurable trend.** You can report the number of open Critical and High findings each month, and show it
  going down.
- **Safe change.** Admins can make changes with the confidence that a mistake will be caught by the next run.

**Subject:** Security assessment request: Maester for Microsoft 365 configuration monitoring

**What it is**

Maester ([maester.dev](https://maester.dev), [source](https://github.com/maester365/maester)) is an open-source
PowerShell module (MIT licence) that reads Microsoft 365, Entra ID and related service configuration and tests it
against built-in and custom checks. It is published on the PowerShell Gallery.

**Business need**

[One or two sentences from the executive or CISO template. Name the risk register entry and the baseline.]

**Access required**

- An identity with read access to Microsoft Graph. `Get-MtGraphScope` lists the exact permissions; by default they are
  all read-only (`*.Read.All` and similar).
- Optional, only if we turn them on: `Mail.Send` to email the report (`-SendMail`), and read-write scopes needed to
  read Global Administrator assignments in PIM (`-Privileged`). [We will / will not use these.]
- For the Exchange Online, Teams and SharePoint tests: [a reader role such as Global Reader / the roles listed in the
  monitoring guide].
- Unattended runs use [a workload identity with federated credentials / a managed identity / a certificate], with no
  stored secret [where possible]. See [Monitoring with Maester](monitoring/readme.mdx).

**Where it runs and where data goes**

- Runs in [our GitHub Actions / Azure DevOps / Azure Automation / an admin workstation], in [region / environment].
- Results (HTML, JSON, optional CSV and Excel) are written to [storage location], with access limited to [group].
  They describe our security configuration and should be classified as [classification].
- User identities can be removed from the outputs with `-RedactUserIdentity`. The list of affected objects is
  collected only with `-IncludeAffectedObjects`.
- Results are sent only where we configure them: [email recipients / a Teams channel / none].
- Telemetry: by default each run sends one usage event, with our tenant ID, to the Maester project's analytics
  service. We will turn this off with `-DisableTelemetry`. [Yes / No]
- With `-SkipVersionCheck` the module makes no calls to check for a newer version.

**Supply chain**

- Source code is public and reviewed through pull requests; each test is a readable PowerShell file.
- We will pin a specific module version, review release notes before upgrading, and install from [the PowerShell
  Gallery / our internal repository].
- Optional Maester Packs are third-party code and are not installed unless we install them. [We will not use packs /
  we will use only (pack) after review.]

**Residual risks and mitigations**

| Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| The monitoring identity is compromised and used to read the tenant's configuration | Read-only permissions, [federated credential / certificate in Key Vault], sign-in monitoring on the identity, Conditional Access for workload identities [if licensed] |
| Reports disclose our security weaknesses | Access-controlled storage, redaction of user identities, retention of [N days] |
| A malicious or faulty module release | Version pinning, review before upgrade, [internal repository] |
| False assurance from passing tests | Maester tests configuration only; it complements, and does not replace, [penetration testing / SIEM / audit] |

**Request**

Assessment and approval to run Maester [version] with the access above, from [environment], by [date].

---

</TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Common questions

**We already have Microsoft Secure Score. Why add this?**
Secure Score is Microsoft's view of recommended settings, and it is worth tracking. Maester adds what Secure Score
does not: tests for your own rules (this group must be in this policy, this app must not have these permissions),
results mapped to the framework you report against, a daily result in your own pipeline with alerts, and the
CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA checks side by side with Maester's own.

**We already have a SIEM, Defender and Sentinel.**
Those watch for activity: sign-ins, alerts, attacks in progress. Maester checks configuration: whether the controls
that prevent those attacks are still in place. A weak setting produces no alert until it is exploited.

**It is free. Who supports it?**
Maester is an open-source project maintained by a community of Microsoft security practitioners, with the source
on [GitHub](https://github.com/maester365/maester). There is no vendor support contract. Because it only reads
configuration and runs in your own environment, the operational risk of a fault is low: the worst case is a run that
fails or a test that reports the wrong result, which you can turn off.

**Will it change anything in our tenant?**
No. By default Maester asks only for read permissions. The optional permissions (sending mail, reading PIM
assignments) are off unless you ask for them.

**How much work is it?**
A first report takes about fifteen minutes. Scheduled monitoring takes a few hours to set up with one of the
[monitoring guides](monitoring/readme.mdx). The ongoing work is fixing what it finds, which is the point.

**We will get hundreds of failures on the first run.**
That is normal, and it is the reason to start. Fix Critical and High first, record the findings you accept as
exceptions with a reason, and report the trend. See [Getting started](getting-started.md#step-3-fix-what-matters-first).

## 📑 Description

Adds three pages to the **Get started** section of the docs for people who are new to Maester, or who need approval to roll it out.

- **Getting started** (`docs/getting-started.md`) takes a reader from a first run to monitoring in seven steps: install and run, read the report (what Passed, Failed, Investigate, Skipped and Error mean), fix Critical and High first (with the quick wins), set up `maester-config.json` (emergency access accounts, accepted exceptions), choose a baseline, monitor and alert, write custom tests.
- **Choosing a baseline** (`docs/choosing-a-baseline.md`) is neutral between frameworks. It lists each suite (Maester, CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA, ORCA, AD) with its source, what it covers and its `-Suite` value. A second table starts from the reader's requirement and names the suites that meet it: CIS evidence, CISA/NIST, Essential Eight/ISM, an internal standard or a framework Maester doesn't ship, identity hardening, email, Zero Trust or hybrid AD. It also covers overlap between suites, saving the choice in `Selection`, recording exceptions in `TestSettings`, and mapping your own tests to your own framework.
- **Making the case for Maester** (`docs/making-the-case.mdx`):
  - A table of 12 configuration failures that go unnoticed without continuous monitoring. Each row says why nobody notices, what it can lead to, and which test catches it.
  - Copy-and-fill templates in tabs for **general executives**, a **CISO** (risk, compliance evidence, metrics, limits) and an **IT Security Adviser (ITSA)**. The ITSA template covers the security assessment of the tool itself: permissions, where it runs, where data goes, telemetry and supply chain.
  - Answers to common questions (Secure Score, SIEM/Defender, support for a free tool).

`intro.mdx` now ends with a "Next steps" section linking to the three pages. They're also added to the Get started group in `astro.config.mjs`.

Every test ID, parameter and permission named on these pages was checked against the current source. This includes the telemetry event in `Write-Telemetry.ps1`, which the ITSA template discloses.

## ✅ Checks

- [x] My pull request adheres to the code style of this project.
- [ ] My code requires changes to the documentation.
- [x] I have updated the documentation as required.

title: Installation guide
---

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

Maester needs **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported.

- Install the **Maester** PowerShell module.

<InstallCommand />

The tests ship inside the module, so there is nothing else to download and no folder to set up.

- Sign into your Microsoft 365 tenant and run the tests.

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

You only need a folder if you want to change settings or add your own tests. Put a `maester-config.json` (see [Configuration](configuration/overview.md)) and a `custom` folder for your tests (see [Writing custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx)) in it, and run `Invoke-Maester -Path <folder>` or run Maester from that folder.

:::note[Pester]
Maester 3.0 does not need Pester. Install it only if you have custom tests written in the Pester format (`*.Tests.ps1`), see [Pester-format tests](writing-tests/pester-format-tests.md):

```powershell
Install-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.7.1 -SkipPublisherCheck -Force -Scope CurrentUser
```

Maester ships on two channels:

- **Stable** releases come out every few weeks. Most people, and most pipelines, should run stable.
- A **preview** is published to the PowerShell Gallery every time a change is merged. It has every new check, command and option as soon as it is merged, before the next stable release.

These docs describe the preview. A check, command or parameter that the stable release doesn't have yet is marked **Preview** on its page and in the [test catalog](/docs/tests). Pick the version you run from the version menu at the top of the page, and the marks say what your version doesn't have.

## Install the preview

```powershell
Install-Module Maester -AllowPrerelease -Force -Scope CurrentUser
```

## 2670 (MT.1265, dynamic groups whose rule processing failed): MERGE once CI has run
Reads the `membershipRuleProcessingStatus` of each active dynamic group (beta) and fails on `Failed`. The fix is to correct the rule. Attributes match the rubric and its sibling MT.1197 (entra/groups/identity-lifecycle, Medium/Low/Low, Mitre None). No other test checks this, so it is not a duplicate. There are no outer try/catch blocks or guards. The only try (`Test.MT.1265.ps1:88-93`) is a deliberate fallback when the CA-reference lookup fails, so the failed groups are still reported. The helpers are in `internal/services/entra/`. The author rebutted CodeRabbit's 404 point well (a 404 means the group was deleted), and CodeRabbit now passes. No maintainer asks are outstanding.
**CI:** build-validation, PSScriptAnalyzer, CodeQL and Build Website are all `action_required` and need approval before merge.

## 2607 (MT.1259, baseline scope sign-ins subject to CA): MERGE once CI has run
Merill's asks (review 2026-10-30), both done:
1. **No stored selection should pass with a note, and be Investigate only when an enabled All-resources policy has an exclusion.** Done at `Test.MT.1259.ps1:123-139`, and the guide's bullets match. One small extension: it is also Investigate when an inactive WAAD exclusion exists. That fits the spirit of the ask.
2. **Title (optional).** Renamed to "Baseline scope sign-ins should be subject to Conditional Access."

Both CodeRabbit asks are fixed (`:93-101` for policies that exclude WAAD only when they include it, `:165-171` for the 403 fallback). The 401/403 try at `:74-82` rethrows other errors, which the writing-tests guide allows. Attributes fit the rubric. MT.1196/1197 don't read baseline scopes, so there is no duplicate. CodeRabbit is paused ("skipping").
**CI:** the same four workflows are `action_required`.

## 2637 (monthly snapshot of agent blocked permissions): CHANGES
What it writes: `powershell/internal/generated/AgentBlockedPermissions.json`. The data comes from the raw markdown of microsoft-graph-docs-contrib; the hash covers only the table, so there is no PR churn. Secrets: `MAESTER_BOT_APP_ID` and `MAESTER_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY`, minted only on change, with contents and PR write. Permissions are `{}` at the top and `contents: read` on the job, with pinned SHAs. This mirrors `update-eam-classification.yaml`, so it is safe.
Main defect: `AgentBlockedPermissionDrift.Tests.ps1:20-33` keeps its own hand copy of MT.1223's 12 permissions. The drift guard can therefore drift itself. It should read the keys from the hashtable in `powershell/internal/services/entra/Get-MtEntraAgentHighRiskGraphPermissionFinding.ps1:6-19` (through the AST, or by splitting the list into its own function).
Minor: the JSON ships in the module, but only a unit test reads it.
Maintainer intent: Merill raised this in #2233 point 4 but left it open ("a refresh path ... or just a documented review cadence"). There is no ruling, so he has to decide whether he wants a new bot workflow. CI is green, and CodeRabbit shows its first major as addressed.
> Thanks @Dfrank77! Nice, careful workflow. One ask: the drift test keeps its own copy of MT.1223's list, so it won't notice when that list changes. Could it read the permissions from `Get-MtEntraAgentHighRiskGraphPermissionFinding` instead (parse the hashtable, or move it into a small function both use)? Then it really ties the two together.

## 2723 (extract the GitHub connection probe): MERGE
This is the refactor Merill asked for on #2633. The logic is unchanged, the headers and connection are passed explicitly, and the helper sits in `internal/services/github/` (one function per file, with help). Tests cover the shared connection identity. There is no cache bypass. CI is green, CodeRabbit found nothing actionable, and Copilot ran out of quota.

## 2670 (MT.1265, dynamic groups whose rule processing failed): MERGE once CI has run
Reads the `membershipRuleProcessingStatus` of each active dynamic group (beta) and fails on `Failed`. The fix is to correct the rule. Attributes match the rubric and its sibling MT.1197 (entra/groups/identity-lifecycle, Medium/Low/Low, Mitre None). No other test checks this, so it is not a duplicate. There are no outer try/catch blocks or guards. The only try (`Test.MT.1265.ps1:88-93`) is a deliberate fallback when the CA-reference lookup fails, so the failed groups are still reported. The helpers are in `internal/services/entra/`. The author rebutted CodeRabbit's 404 point well (a 404 means the group was deleted), and CodeRabbit now passes. No maintainer asks are outstanding.
**CI:** build-validation, PSScriptAnalyzer, CodeQL and Build Website are all `action_required` and need approval before merge.

## 2607 (MT.1259, baseline scope sign-ins subject to CA): MERGE once CI has run
Merill's asks (review 2026-10-30), both done:
1. **No stored selection should pass with a note, and be Investigate only when an enabled All-resources policy has an exclusion.** Done at `Test.MT.1259.ps1:123-139`, and the guide's bullets match. One small extension: it is also Investigate when an inactive WAAD exclusion exists. That fits the spirit of the ask.
2. **Title (optional).** Renamed to "Baseline scope sign-ins should be subject to Conditional Access."

Both CodeRabbit asks are fixed (`:93-101` for policies that exclude WAAD only when they include it, `:165-171` for the 403 fallback). The 401/403 try at `:74-82` rethrows other errors, which the writing-tests guide allows. Attributes fit the rubric. MT.1196/1197 don't read baseline scopes, so there is no duplicate. CodeRabbit is paused ("skipping").
**CI:** the same four workflows are `action_required`.

## 2637 (monthly snapshot of agent blocked permissions): CHANGES
What it writes: `powershell/internal/generated/AgentBlockedPermissions.json`. The data comes from the raw markdown of microsoft-graph-docs-contrib; the hash covers only the table, so there is no PR churn. Secrets: `MAESTER_BOT_APP_ID` and `MAESTER_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY`, minted only on change, with contents and PR write. Permissions are `{}` at the top and `contents: read` on the job, with pinned SHAs. This mirrors `update-eam-classification.yaml`, so it is safe.
Main defect: `AgentBlockedPermissionDrift.Tests.ps1:20-33` keeps its own hand copy of MT.1223's 12 permissions. The drift guard can therefore drift itself. It should read the keys from the hashtable in `powershell/internal/services/entra/Get-MtEntraAgentHighRiskGraphPermissionFinding.ps1:6-19` (through the AST, or by splitting the list into its own function).
Minor: the JSON ships in the module, but only a unit test reads it.
Maintainer intent: Merill raised this in #2233 point 4 but left it open ("a refresh path ... or just a documented review cadence"). There is no ruling, so he has to decide whether he wants a new bot workflow. CI is green, and CodeRabbit shows its first major as addressed.
> Thanks @Dfrank77! Nice, careful workflow. One ask: the drift test keeps its own copy of MT.1223's list, so it won't notice when that list changes. Could it read the permissions from `Get-MtEntraAgentHighRiskGraphPermissionFinding` instead (parse the hashtable, or move it into a small function both use)? Then it really ties the two together.
